summary: Specifies the process the IESG uses to decide whether a MIB specification meets the requirements for advancing on the IETF standards track, and gives the reasons for that process. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: This explains the checklist that decides whether a document describing network gauges has been tested enough to move up to the next grade.

questions: how do mib specifications advance on the standards track
what is a mib implementation report
how does the iesg test mib interoperability
subtitle: How the IESG decides whether a MIB specification has been implemented enough to move up the standards track.

tldr.problem: The Internet Standards Process requires multiple, independent, interoperable implementations before a specification can advance past Proposed Standard, but it is unclear what interoperation means for a MIB, which is a data dictionary rather than a protocol with state machines.
tldr.mechanism: Each MIB specification put forward for advancement needs one or more advocates who argue convincingly that the requirements are met, backed by an implementation report that normally includes basic object comparison testing.
tldr.outcome: The IESG gets a practical test instead of exhaustive testing: the goal is a clear specification and the removal of features that nobody implemented.

today: RFC 2438 is a Best Current Practice, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes the process as of 1998, when the IESG used it to judge MIB specifications for advancement.

sections.title: Why Interoperability Is Required
sections.content:
The Internet Standards Process (RFC 2026) requires that a specification have multiple, independent, and interoperable implementations before it can advance beyond Proposed Standard. At least two genetically unrelated implementations must be shown to interoperate correctly with all features and options.

The RFC gives two reasons. The first is to verify that the text of the specification is clear and accurate: if several efforts built interoperable implementations from it, it probably is. The second is to discourage excessive options and feature creep. If an option is not in at least two interoperable implementations, it is safe to assume nobody found it useful, and it must be removed before the specification can advance.
sections.eli5: Two teams building the same toy from the same instructions is the test. If both toys work together, the instructions are clear, and parts nobody built can be dropped.

sections.title: What Makes a MIB Different
sections.content:
For a protocol that defines the bits on the wire exchanged by state machines, interoperability is intuitive: the implementations must talk to each other while using all features and options. For an SNMP Management Information Base (MIB), what counts as interoperation is less obvious.

A MIB specification is data oriented. Data types and instance definitions greatly outnumber procedural or causal rules between objects. It also does not stand alone, because it is the access interface to the instrumentation underneath it. Without that instrumentation, a MIB has form but no values. The RFC says a MIB looks more like an API or a dictionary than a state machine protocol.

It also separates two things: judging applications that use MIBs, which can be black-box tested, and judging the MIBs themselves, which are not readily amenable to black-box test plans.
sections.eli5: A MIB is like a dictionary or a list of gauges on a dashboard. A dictionary has no moving parts to test, so checking it needs a different approach than checking a machine.

sections.title: The Recommended Process
sections.content:
The Operations and Management Area Directors and the IESG must be convinced that a MIB advancing to Draft Standard or Internet Standard is clearly written, has multiple interoperable implementations, and has had all options implemented. The RFC considers the very thorough approaches (full coverage and stimulus-response testing) too costly to be reasonable in practice, so it adopts a more pragmatic process.

Each MIB specification suggested for advancement must have one or more advocates who can make a convincing argument that the multiple implementation and feature support requirements are met. How the argument is made is left to the advocate, but it will normally include reports that basic object comparison testing has been done.

The recommendation must come with an implementation report, as for any advancement request. It must say why the IESG should believe there are multiple implementations and that all MIB objects are supported in more than one of them. The IESG's prime concern is the underlying reasons: a clear and unambiguous text, and removal of features that have not garnered support.

The report is placed on the IETF web page with other pre-advancement reports and is referred to in the IETF Last-Call. The Area Director(s) of the relevant Area decide whether it is adequate, and that decision can be challenged during the Last-Call period.
sections.eli5: Someone has to stand up and prove, with a written report, that at least two teams built it and that every part got used. A grown-up judge reads the report, and anyone can object before the final decision.

sections.title: Testing Approaches Considered
sections.content:
An appendix lists the models the IESG debated. It is not exhaustive, but it captures the major plausible ones.

  • Basic Object Comparison: take two unrelated implementations, an SNMP agent and a management station able to do a MIB Dump (extract the complete set of object types and values). Compare the two dumps to check that both provide all mandatory and optional objects and that objects have the correct types.
  • Stimulus/Response Testing: as above, but also exercise the two network elements so that all objects show plausible values in operational conditions. A stricter reading would require the objects to track identically under identical stimulus. The RFC notes that the underlying instrumentation is an application that uses the MIB, not part of the MIB.
  • Full Coverage Testing: treat the MIB as an API and exercise all paths through the causal semantics, verifying that all objects change state correctly. Again, much more than the MIB definition is being tested.

The first is what the recommended process normally relies on. The RFC judges the other two to be beyond what can reasonably be accomplished.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to check: compare two lists of gauges, poke the machines and watch the gauges move, or test every possible situation. The first is quick and the last is far too much work.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC acknowledges that some may see this policy as lowering the confidence people can have in MIB specifications. The O&M Area Directors and the IESG believe it still ensures a reasonable evaluation of how clear a MIB specification is, and that unused options can be identified and removed before advancement.

It adds that good, clearly written MIB specifications help manage the Internet and other networks, and so help reduce some types of security threats.
sections.eli5: Some people worry that a lighter check means less trust. The authors say it is still a good check, and clear gauge rules help keep networks safe.

references.text: Bradner, S., "The Internet Standards Process -- Revision 3", BCP 9, RFC 2026, October 1996.
